title: Part VI — ALIGNMENT: Decisions and Planning

know: The part answers three questions in order, one per chapter: By what method are decision rights allocated, and how is a decision recorded so that it lasts?; How do capacity planning and outcome planning fit into one process?; Which recurring forums and written artefacts does an organization need at each size?
can_do: Pick the chapter of this part that answers the question in front of them.

audience.who: Executives and individual contributors in product and tech who have read Parts I to V and are about to start Part VI, or who arrive with one question about decisions, planning or recurring meetings and want the chapter that answers it.
already_knows: Quarterly planning, budgets, roadmaps, team goals and recurring meetings as they are usually run.

Parts I to V in outline: work, information and decisions as the flows of an organization and the working definition of a decision right (chapter 1), the vision-led roadmap of Part III, the engineering strategy and decision record of Part IV, and the leadership structure of Part V.
does_not_know: Alignment as the result of mechanisms and not of culture; defined here.
Allocating a decision right and the content of a decision record (chapter 22); glossed here.
The financial plan, allocation and team objectives as separate planning steps (chapter 23); glossed here.
Forum, written artefact and operating cadence (chapter 24); glossed here.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the three chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next three chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Decision Rights and Decision Records; Planning; Operating Cadence.

thesis.question: How do many teams decide and plan so that their work adds up?
thesis.claim: Alignment is produced by three explicit mechanisms: decision rights that put each decision next to its information and record it, a planning process in which capacity allocation and outcome selection are separate steps joined by team objectives, and a small set of recurring forums and written artefacts that carry information along designed paths.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that alignment comes from a shared culture and frequent communication, so that process is a substitute for trust and should be kept to a minimum.
thesis.so_what: A leader who finds teams pulling apart looks for the missing decision right, the tangled planning step or the absent forum before calling for better communication.
thesis.how_why: Information and the right to decide are separated by default as an organization grows; a decision right rejoins them, a plan makes many teams' decisions consistent in advance, and a forum moves the information the next decision needs. Each is a designed path for one of the flows of chapter 1, and none arises from goodwill alone.

supporting_claims.claim: A decision right puts a named kind of decision with the role that has the information, says whose advice is required and where the decision is recorded, and a recorded decision is what lets the next one build on it.
Planning works when the financial plan, the allocation of capacity and the choice of outcomes are decided in that order and separately, with team objectives as the contract between leaders and teams.
An organization needs a small, sized set of recurring forums and written artefacts, each with an owner and a decision or information flow it exists for.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis and the reading order.

additional_patterns.applies_to: three-mechanisms and the chapter list in the closing: decision rights, then planning, then the operating cadence

flow.rationale: The page opens on a planning cycle that took nine of the quarter's thirteen weeks and still left three teams building the same integration, and on the question of which decisions planning is made of. The first section says why alignment does not arise by itself as an organization grows, and why asking for it does not produce it; the second gives the three mechanisms that produce it and says why they come in that order; the chapter list closes the page. The cause stands before the mechanisms because each mechanism is justified by the separation it repairs; put the mechanisms first and decision rights, planning steps and forums arrive as process for its own sake, which is the objection the part disputes. The list comes last because a reader can choose a chapter only after seeing what each mechanism does.

hook.content: In 2026 Corvane's quarterly planning took nine of the quarter's thirteen weeks, and at the end of it three teams were building the same integration.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader's experience of planning that consumes the time it plans.
bridge.to_topic: The question that experience raises and that the usual answers (communicate more, or cut the process and trust people) skip: which decisions planning is made of.

thesis_statement.text: Part VI argues that alignment is produced by three explicit mechanisms: decision rights that put each decision next to its information and record it, a planning process in which capacity allocation and outcome selection are separate steps joined by team objectives, and a small set of recurring forums and written artefacts that carry information along designed paths.

promises.promise: Why alignment does not arise by itself as an organization grows.

The three mechanisms that produce alignment and why they come in that order; three chapters answer three questions in order: who decides what and how the decision is recorded, how capacity and outcomes are planned in one process, and which forums and documents an organization needs at each size.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2026 Corvane's quarterly planning took nine of the quarter's thirteen weeks, and at the end of it three teams were building the same integration.

evidence.what: Corvane (fictional): in 2026, at about 500 people and about thirty teams in four product groups, quarterly planning took nine of the quarter's thirteen weeks, negotiated across budget, headcount, roadmap and team goals in meetings with every director; at the end three teams were building the same integration.
evidence.shows: A great deal of time spent aligning that did not align the work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Planning that consumes the time it plans is usually answered with more communication or with less process and more trust, and the question both answers skip is which decisions planning is made of; at Corvane nobody could list them, because budget, headcount, roadmap and team goals were negotiated together.

evidence.what: Nine weeks of meetings is already a great deal of communication, so more of it is not the missing thing; and with less process the three teams would still not have known of each other. What nobody could say is which decisions the nine weeks were for, who made each and where it was written down.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json, part-6 opening bridge and disputed_by
evidence.shows: Why neither more communication nor less process addresses the cause.

transition_in.carries_over: Corvane's nine weeks and the three teams.
transition_in.introduces: The reader's own version of that planning, the two usual answers, and the question that both skip.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part VI argues that alignment is produced by three explicit mechanisms (decision rights, a planning process of separate steps, and a small set of forums and written artefacts), and it makes the argument in three chapters that answer three questions in order.

sections.heading: Why Asking for Alignment Does Not Produce It
sections.controlling_idea: As an organization grows, information and the right to decide are separated by default, which leaves three things missing (a decider with the information, consistency between many teams' decisions, and a path for the information the next decision needs), and goodwill and communication do not supply them.

advances_thesis.how: States the reasoning from which the part derives its three mechanisms.

transition_in.carries_over: The part's claim as stated in the lead.
transition_in.introduces: The reasoning that produces it: what growth separates, and what is then missing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: As an organization grows, the information a decision needs and the right to make it are separated by default, and three things are then missing: a decider who has the information, consistency between the decisions of many teams, and a path by which the information the next decision needs reaches the person deciding.

evidence.what: Information and the right to decide are separated by default as an organization grows; a decision right rejoins them, a plan makes many teams' decisions consistent in advance, and a forum moves the information the next decision needs.
evidence.shows: What is missing in a grown organization, stated before any mechanism is named, so that each mechanism in the next section arrives as the repair of one gap.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shared culture and frequent communication do not supply the three missing things by themselves, because informal coordination covers only the paths between people who already talk and leaves out the paths the organization needs and nobody walks; so the paths have to be designed.

evidence.what: Informal coordination covers the paths between people who already talk and leaves out the paths the design needs and nobody walks. None of the three missing things arises from goodwill alone.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json, part-6 how_why and disputed_by, and the how_why of operating-cadence
evidence.shows: Why the part does not treat process as a substitute for trust.

transition_in.introduces: The common view that culture and communication supply them unaided, and where it falls short.

sections.heading: Three Mechanisms of Alignment
sections.controlling_idea: The part builds alignment from three mechanisms (decision rights with records, planning in separate steps joined by team objectives, and an operating cadence of forums and written artefacts), and they come in the order in which each needs the one before.

advances_thesis.how: One list item per supporting claim, then the order.

flow.rationale: Decision rights come first because planning is a set of decisions that needs them, and the cadence comes last because its forums exist to make the decisions and carry the plans the first two chapters define. The paragraph on the order closes the section because the dependency can be stated only once all three mechanisms have been met; cadence first would be a calendar of meetings with nothing to decide.

transition_in.carries_over: The three missing things, which goodwill does not supply.
transition_in.introduces: The three mechanisms that supply them, one per chapter.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three mechanisms supply the three missing things, each a designed path for one of the flows of chapter 1: a decision right, which puts a named kind of decision with the role that has the information, says whose advice is required and where the decision is recorded; planning, in which the financial plan, the allocation of capacity and the choice of outcomes are decided in that order and separately, with team objectives as the contract between leaders and teams; and an operating cadence, a small set of recurring forums and written artefacts, each with an owner and a decision or information flow it exists for, which moves the information the next decision needs; the plan is what makes many teams' decisions consistent in advance.

advances_thesis.how: Names the three mechanisms with their terms glossed, one per supporting claim.

evidence.what: Planning as a financial plan, an allocation and a roadmap (Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer, 2024); the roadmap derived from a vision and outcomes (Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters, 2020).
evidence.source: journal-spec.json entries of chapters 22 to 24; PLAN.md anchors
evidence.shows: That the planning steps are named sources' models, which chapter 23 presents and joins.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three mechanisms come in prerequisite order, decision rights first because planning is a set of decisions that needs them and the cadence last because its forums exist to make those decisions and carry those plans; each mechanism is a designed path, which is the book's system-design lens, and has users by whom it is judged, which is its product-thinking lens, and planning is where the product model of Part III and the engineering model of Part IV meet.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the three supporting claims as mechanisms that depend on each other.

evidence.what: Planning is a set of decisions that needs decision rights; the cadence's forums exist to make the decisions and carry the plans; cadence first would be a calendar of meetings with nothing to decide. Larson's model answers how much capacity goes where and Build What Matters answers what it is for, so planning is where Parts III and IV meet. Each mechanism has users, the people who decide and the teams that wait for a decision, and is kept only while it serves them.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json, part-6 flow rationale, role and the entry of planning
evidence.shows: Why the chapters are read in this order, and why the middle one is the book's central joint.

transition_in.introduces: The one direction in which they depend on each other, and where the book's two lenses and the two earlier operating models appear in them.

conclusion.heading: Chapters in this part
conclusion.synthesis: Read in order, the three chapters follow a decision from who makes it, through the plan that many such decisions add up to, to the rhythm of meetings and documents in which decisions and plans are made and carried.
conclusion.so_what: A leader who finds teams pulling apart looks for the missing decision right, the tangled planning step or the absent forum before calling for better communication.

callback.to: Corvane's nine weeks of quarterly planning and the three teams building the same integration from the opening (p01).
callback.how: The closing reads the nine weeks against the lead's question: nobody at Corvane had said which decisions the nine weeks were for, so the planning could run long and still leave three teams on the same integration.

The three chapters follow a decision from who makes it, through the plan, to the rhythm that carries both; at Corvane nobody had said which decisions the nine weeks were for; a leader who has the three answers looks for the missing decision right, the tangled planning step or the absent forum before calling for better communication, and the first chapter starts with the first mechanism, who decides and how the decision is kept.
